name: Aaron Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the billing queue at a contact centre and handle the cases that come back after a credit was refused. I have a two-year college diploma and use AI search every day, though I check account dates myself before promising money. I like finding the mistake that stops a third call; Saturdays I fix friends' bicycles for the pleasure of working with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor the small AI tools are another way to find an old case faster. I'd still want us to check the customer’s account before promising a credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day, so a small improvement is ordinary to me. My lead pay is good for this work and I've saved about nine months of expenses; a slow year would leave me room to choose my next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the complex billing calls and record which search suggestions actually save time. In the first year of this plateau, I'd put a fixed amount into savings each payday and keep my Saturday bicycle repairs as a hobby, not a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. I still have to run a busy team, but a slight change in software doesn't take away the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why measure the search suggestions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a suggested answer pointed to an old price, and I caught it before a refund went out. If I track errors as well as speed, I can tell my manager when a shortcut is worth using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the repairs as a hobby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like fixing bikes for friends, but I make more on my lead shift than a new repair bench would bring in. My savings are for choices, not for pretending every hobby needs a shop.

S0.quote: My savings are for choices, not for pretending every hobby needs a shop.
say: I would call small AI tools a way to find **old cases** faster.
I would ask agents to check the **account** before promising a credit.
think: I use AI daily and see a **small improvement** as ordinary.
I earn strong lead pay and have **nine months** saved, giving me room to choose.
do: Keep handling **complex billing** calls and tracking useful search suggestions.
Transfer a fixed amount into **savings** each payday.
Keep **Saturday bicycle repairs** as a hobby while lead work pays better.
feel: **Comfortable** with the job and household money.
fieldNote: Aaron tests shortcuts by **errors and speed**, rather than assuming a fast answer is right.
He resists turning a **hobby** into a business while his lead role pays well.

steps.text: Keep leading complex billing calls and Saturday hobby repairs
Track AI search errors and time saved on billing cases
Move a fixed amount from each payday into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team that faster chats will mean new targets, so we should see the numbers before cheering. I'd offer to run a trial on the repeat cases and share the results with agents and managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my paid day is thinking work on a screen, and a smaller team could include my own post. I have savings and several other centres nearby. I don't want to mistake a cushion for a job guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd compare fifty repeat chats with AI drafts and count wrong credits, not just response time. During the first year after rollout, if our centre cuts lead shifts, I'd apply for a posted service quality role at another local centre; I'd ask for its pay and hours before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, with an edge to it. I can handle a job search, but I would miss the team I've built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a second agent to check the same fifty cases without seeing my scores. A system that finishes the easy ones faster but causes repeat calls hasn't saved us much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the agents whose chats disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know how many places the company will keep. I'd share the trial results and the local vacancies I see, rather than promise everyone a testing badge.

S1.quote: I don't want to mistake a cushion for a job guarantee.
say: I would ask to see **new targets** before celebrating faster chats.
I would share a **repeat-case trial** with agents and managers.
think: I know a smaller team could include my **lead post** because screen work changes first.
I have **savings and local options**, but neither guarantees another good job.
do: Compare fifty **repeat chats** with AI drafts and count wrong credits.
Apply for a posted **service quality** role elsewhere if lead shifts are cut.
Check **pay and hours** before giving notice at my centre.
feel: **Curious** about the tool, uneasy about a smaller team.
fieldNote: Aaron specifies **wrong credits** as a trial measure, rather than relying on response speed.
His local options and savings support a **measured search**, not an impulsive resignation.

steps.text: Compare fifty repeat chats with AI drafts and count wrong credits
Apply for a posted local service quality role if lead shifts fall
Check offered pay and hours before resigning from the current centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should tell staff when decisions will be made, while there is still time to plan. I wouldn't sell an AI checking role as a safe landing when the system can do most thinking work itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could replace the billing judgment I am paid extra for. Robots around 2031 might even learn the hands-on bicycle work I enjoy, so a repair shop is not a secure escape. Nine months saved lets me experiment, but it can still run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask management for a dated staffing plan now and stop adding expensive parts to my hobby bench. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my role ends, I'd take paid repair shifts at a local cycle shop if one is advertised, and use no more than one month of savings for an accredited repair course after checking the fee and whether robots are already changing the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yes, but I can move. The short clock makes me protect the savings that give me options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cap the course spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course that uses half my reserve to reach work that robots may soon do would be a poor bet. I would visit the shop first and ask what repairs still need a person before I pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any contact centre opening first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a centre offer with real wages and hours as a bridge if my own place closed. I wouldn't call it a ten-year plan, because AGI reaches those calls too.

S2.quote: A course that uses half my reserve to reach work that robots may soon do would be a poor bet.
say: I would ask for a **dated staffing plan** before the centre changes jobs.
I would refuse to call **AI checking** a guaranteed safe landing.
think: I could lose my **billing judgment** work to AGI by 2028.
I know **2031 robots** may reach bicycle repairs too, so nine months saved cannot fund blind bets.
do: Ask management for a **staffing date** and stop buying costly hobby parts now.
Take advertised **paid repair shifts** if my lead role ends.
Take an **accredited repair course** only after checking fees, robot use, and a one-month savings cap.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to protect savings and try paid work.
fieldNote: Aaron rejects the tempting claim that **bike repair** stays safe once hands-on robots arrive around 2031.
His **one-month cap** makes the strong cushion an experiment budget rather than unlimited tuition.

steps.text: Stop buying expensive bicycle parts for the hobby bench
Take advertised paid cycle shop shifts after a lead role cut
Take an accredited repair course only after fee and robot checks within a one-month cap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough to test a different line of work without giving up our wages today. I would ask management for annual staffing numbers, because guesses about a distant date are not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could try paid cycle shop shifts before 2031 and see whether I enjoy repairs as work. Thinking AI still reaches the centre in 2031, and robots follow around 2034, so I would not sign a long shop lease on today's tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the local cycle shop about a paid weekend shift and keep my lead job. If the shop has a real opening and I like the work, I'd take a short repair course using no more than one month of savings; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd choose the better paid role still available and keep the rest of my reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More patient than in the fast case. Five years lets me learn whether the bike work is more than a Saturday pleasure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a good weekend test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to handle a full queue of punctures and brake repairs and see the shop's actual pay sheet. Friends thanking me for a free fix is not proof that I can earn a living from repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the centre role so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre pays well and there are other centres nearby. I'd keep that income until I have paid work elsewhere, even while testing a second route.

S3.quote: Friends thanking me for a free fix is not proof that I can earn a living from repairs.
say: I would ask for **annual staffing numbers** and a chance to test other work while still employed.
I would say five years allows **paid trials**, rather than an immediate exit.
think: I could test **paid bike repairs** before AGI reaches the centre in 2031.
I would avoid a **long shop lease** because hands-on robots arrive around 2034.
do: Ask a local cycle shop for a **paid weekend opening** this year.
Keep my **lead job** until another role pays real wages.
Take a **short repair course** if a paid opening works out, within one month of savings.
feel: **Patient**, because the longer runway allows a real work test.
fieldNote: Aaron distinguishes free favours from a **paid queue** with actual wages.
He treats the **2034 robot date** as a reason to avoid a long lease, not a reason to freeze.

steps.text: Apply for a paid weekend shift at the local cycle shop if advertised
Keep leading billing calls until another role pays real wages
Take a short repair course if paid shop work suits him within a one-month cap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to check where the service work is going and to try another trade without panic. I'd ask the centre to publish its staffing plan each year, not just launch a new dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I may have moved into a shop or another centre, and I can save more before deciding. The same AGI still reaches call work first; the 2039 robots make bike repairs a business risk, so owning a shop outright would be a big leap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the lead shift for now and shadow the cycle shop on a paid weekend if it offers one. Over the decade I'd put money into a course fund and take a short accredited class only if paid repair work keeps coming; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd move to the best real offer rather than sign a shop lease just because the centre changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Ten years is enough for several careful tests, and my reserve keeps any one test from deciding my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a best offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare full-year wages, hours, and whether the employer pays for training. The title matters less to me than being able to cover rent without draining savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a shop if repairs went well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until I had years of actual customers and knew what robots were doing in repair work. A paid shift tells me more than a glossy plan for a shop.

S4.quote: A paid shift tells me more than a glossy plan for a shop.
say: I would ask the centre for **yearly staffing plans** as tools change.
I would say a decade allows **work trials** without a rushed exit.
think: I could save more or move jobs before **2036 AGI** changes call work.
I see **2039 robots** making shop ownership risky even if repair shifts pay.
do: Keep my **lead shift** and take a paid shop weekend only if offered.
Build a **course fund** over the decade.
Take an **accredited class** only if paid repair work continues.
feel: **Steady**, with time and savings for several small tests.
fieldNote: Aaron tests opportunities against **yearly wages** rather than an appealing job title.
He refuses a **shop lease** until paid demand and robot effects are clearer.

steps.text: Keep leading billing calls while full shifts remain
Compare wages, hours and training support; change jobs after 2036 only for rent-covering wages
Add money to a repair course fund over the decade
Take an accredited repair class only if paid shop work continues

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking work I am paid well for could vanish before I can test a new line of work. A dated staffing plan and paid trials at another employer would help. I have nine months saved, but I want that money to buy choices rather than cover a bad guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a wrong credit when every reply sounds convincing. Customers need a route to a person with the account history, whether that person is me or somebody else.

headlineQuote: I have nine months saved, but I want that money to buy choices rather than cover a bad guess.
portrait: Aaron, **27**, leads complex billing calls and uses AI daily while checking account dates against its suggestions.
He has a **two-year diploma**, higher pay, nine months saved, and plenty of nearby contact centres.
He enjoys **bicycle repairs**, but tests paid shop shifts and fees before treating the hobby as a job.
The **2028 AGI** clock worries him most; longer runways let him try paid work before risking a course or lease.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the billing judgment that earns his higher pay before he can test another line of work.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated staffing plan** and paid work trials would let him use savings for choices rather than a blind course.
